questions.direct_answer: A multi-stage Dockerfile uses one stage to compile a Go program and another to run it. `COPY --from=build` transfers only selected artifacts, so compilers, source files, and build caches do not have to ship in production. Docker builds the dependency graph needed by the selected target; the final stage receives only files explicitly copied from earlier stages.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A multi-stage Dockerfile uses one stage to compile a Go program and another to run it. `COPY --from=build` transfers only selected artifacts, so compilers, source files, and build caches do not have to ship in production.

Stages have separate filesystems and may use different base images. Docker builds the dependency graph needed by the selected target; the final stage receives only files explicitly copied from earlier stages.

For example, the first stage compiles `./cmd/api` to `/out/api`; the final stage copies that file and CA certificates, selects a non-root user, and launches `/api`. Source code and the Go compiler remain outside the runtime image.

Smaller does not automatically mean safer or easier to operate. The chosen runtime base still needs security updates, a usable non-root identity, and every file the program reads. Platform and CGO settings must match the destination.

Use multiple stages when build dependencies are larger or more privileged than the runtime needs. This is a natural fit for Go because many services can be compiled into one executable, sometimes with CGO disabled.

sections.title: The core model: a multi-stage Docker build for Go
sections.content:
a multi-stage Docker build for Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

Multi-stage construction reduces the gap between a rich compiler environment and a focused runtime. The builder may contain compilers, source, Git metadata, and caches. The production stage needs only what the process reads or executes. This separation also prevents accidental reliance on a tool that exists during compilation but not after deployment. Go's static-linking story depends on the program: pure-Go packages can often build with `CGO_ENABLED=0`, while database drivers or native libraries may require CGO and matching system libraries. Cross-compilation adds another dimension because `GOOS` and `GOARCH` must match the runtime platform. BuildKit cache mounts can speed repeated module or build-cache use without copying those caches into the image. The reliable test is therefore not image size alone. Start the final image, exercise TLS, time zones, file access, health endpoints, and graceful shutdown under the same platform and security settings used in deployment.

sections.title: a multi-stage Docker build for Go flow
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Source + modules] --> B[Builder stage]
  B --> C[Compiled binary]
  C --> D[Runtime stage]
  B -. toolchain and cache stay behind .-> E[Not shipped]
```

sections.title: a multi-stage Docker build for Go example
sections.content:
~~~dockerfile
FROM golang:1.25 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -o /out/api ./cmd/api

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/
COPY --from=build /out/api /api
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]
~~~

sections.title: a multi-stage Docker build for Go at a glance
sections.content:
| Concern | Builder stage | Runtime stage |
|---|---|---|
| Compiler | Required | Usually absent |
| Source | Required | Usually absent |
| Binary | Produced | Required |
| Certificates/libraries | Build-dependent | Required when program uses them |
